## Proof of effort

ArXiv recently implemented strict penalties for any author(s) submitting preprints with incontravertible evidence of AI usage. They have not (and should not!) made any policies around text that is suspected of AI usage, and it seems that in the near future you will be regularly, unknowingly reading AI-generated text across scientific domains [footnote: One might hope that crowdsourcing might help with this, for example using upvotes as evidence that an abstract is human-written. This is not the case: ??????]. This all requires serious attention and debate, and for now I will just leave some random thoughts:

 - Can we please note waste eachother's time? If you do feel obligated to put in effort to summarize your research and its impact, why should I spend my time and energy on understanding what you've done?
  - If you don't want to write an abstract, then don't! Richard Hamming, who lived through and propelled widespread adoption of early scientific computing, said something like, "The product of automatation is equivalent but different than what you are automating". Instead of using LLMs to fill in the blanks of a typical research paper, go come up with a better form of research automation!
  - Just because generating scientific text is not explicitly banned, does not mean that it is okay! It is antisocial, actually. If you found out that your colleague was communicating to you via an AI agent, would you think that colleague values your time? Would you think what they had to say was any more valuable than prompting an AI for answers yourself? I will make the same exact update if I find out your scientific writing is AI-generated.
